title: Conversion practices, family conversations and the courts
label: 19 November 2026 · Families and the draft ban
summary: The committee examined how the draft ban on abusive conversion practices might work in families and family courts. Des Johnson welcomed protection for LGBT people and argued that the Bill targets deliberate attempts to change someone, not difficult parenting conversations. Matilda Gosling feared that its wording could discourage parents and professionals from exploring a young person’s gender identity. Family-law witnesses did not take a position for or against the Bill, but urged clearer language, careful rules for protection orders and resources for already stretched courts. The witnesses disagreed about the scale of unintended risks, but several supported making the Bill clearer.

speakers.label: Sarah Branson
speakers.name: Sarah Branson
speakers.role: Family-law barrister and member of the Family Law Bar Association

speakers.label: Des Johnson
speakers.name: Des Johnson
speakers.role: Chair of trustees, FFLAG, a charity supporting families of LGBT people

speakers.label: Shabana Jaffar
speakers.name: Shabana Jaffar
speakers.role: Head of legal, CAFCASS, the Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service

glossary.definition: A legal test used when deciding whether the state may intervene to protect a child from harm caused by their care.
A family-court order giving a local authority powers over a child's care, potentially including where the child lives.
Changing how someone presents and is treated socially in relation to gender, without necessarily receiving medical treatment.
A court order intended to prevent a harmful practice, rather than only responding after harm has occurred.
A council with responsibilities that include investigating risks to children and arranging child protection.

chapters.title: What the Bill would cover
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses agreed that the wording matters, but differed sharply on whether it protects children without drawing in ordinary family life.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are the Bill’s definitions of an abusive conversion practice and serious harm or distress clear enough, especially for families?

evidence.quote: Are the definitions of “abusive conversion practice” and “serious harm, alarm or distress” sufficiently clear, particularly in how they would apply in family settings?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Not to me as a family lawyer. Courts already use a test called “significant harm” when deciding whether the state can intervene in family life. I can’t tell whether this Bill sets a higher or lower test, or means to use the same one.

evidence.quote: We are very familiar with terms such as “significant harm”. That is not the language of this Act, and therefore I am not clear whether it is the intention of Parliament in drafting this Act that there would be a different test for intervention in family life if the issue of conversion practices is engaged or whether it is drafting that is meant to replicate “significant harm”, but that is not what it says.
I do not know whether the test is less or more than evidence of “significant harm”.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: FFLAG welcomes the Bill. We believe it addresses abuse that current law doesn’t cover, and that both sexual orientation and gender identity deserve protection. In the 2018 national LGBT survey, 2% of respondents said they’d undergone conversion practices; among trans respondents it was 4%.

evidence.quote: FFLAG and I believe the Bill is very welcome. It tackles a very specific form of abuse that is not covered elsewhere under current legislation.

We welcome that it offers protection on the basis of both sexual orientation and gender identity. We are well aware they are different, but they are both equally worthy of protection from abuse and harm, in our opinion.

Of the 108,000 respondents to the 2018 national LGBT survey, which is the most authoritative source that we seem to have available, 2% had undergone conversion practices. That rises to 4% for trans people

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: I’d change four things. Include attempts to suppress someone’s identity as well as change it. Limit the healthcare exemption so just anyone can’t claim it. Distinguish practices meeting the Bill’s criminal test from other practices we also consider abusive. And cover conduct likely to cause serious harm or distress, not only harm already caused.

evidence.quote: In clause 1(2), we think you should add suppression. Suppression is just as harmful as change

we are very comfortable that there is a healthcare exemption, but it needs to be limited in scope to professionals who are regulated by a statutory regulatory body or listed on a register held by an organisation accredited by the Professional Standards Authority. Otherwise, anybody could claim that healthcare exemption
all conversion practices are abuse and are abusive, but not all of them will meet the threshold of abuse laid out in the Bill.
we ask you to add “or is likely to cause” alongside the definitions for serious harm, serious alarm and distress.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I’m particularly concerned about children and gender identity. Unlike sexual orientation, a young person’s gender identity can lead towards medical treatment with lasting effects. Their circumstances, including trauma or discomfort with gender stereotypes, might also need exploring. I worry the Bill could treat that exploration as an attempt to change them.

evidence.quote: I am concerned about the definitions of abusive conversion practices as they relate to gender identity specifically, and particularly in the context of children and young people.

gender identity brings risks of long-term physical and mental health effects through a medicalisation pathway. The Bill also overlooks the relevance of social context, trauma and reasons other than an innate, immutable identity, for which somebody might identify as transgender.
The Bill potentially makes an abusive conversion practice of helping children and young people feel comfort in their body, or helping them feel that they do not have to conform to stereotypes.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: The Bill doesn’t separate adults from children. Terms such as “psychological or emotional pressure” could be hard to distinguish from ordinary, sometimes imperfect parenting. Teenagers can also experience serious distress for many reasons.

evidence.quote: There is also a problem with the definitions, in that the Bill does not distinguish between adults and children.
“psychological or emotional pressure” has not been defined. It would be very difficult to separate ordinary parenting from that.

“serious alarm or distress”, which I think most teenagers feel from time to time over very many issues. It would be very difficult to draw that out in a way that would enable criminalisation of parents and other interested adults.

chapters.title: A challenge over gender identity
chapters.takeaway: Danny Beales questioned why Gosling’s concerns about young people’s circumstances should change how the Bill treats conversion practices.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Why does a young trans person’s experience of trauma mean conversion practices should be treated differently? Gay, lesbian and bisexual young people can experience mental health problems, homelessness and trauma too.

evidence.quote: you suggested that trans people experience trauma and sexual abuse, and therefore conversion practices may or not be relevant.
Are you aware of the level of mental health issues, homelessness and trauma in the LGB community? One could make similar arguments for gay, lesbian and bisexual children.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: Trauma could be a factor in how someone comes to identify as transgender, and might need exploring. Children who’d been in care were, according to the figures I cited, much more common among adolescents referred to the former gender identity service. I’m not aware of comparable research about being in care among lesbian, gay and bisexual people, though I may be wrong.

evidence.quote: it can potentially be a factor in their transgender identification, which may then need further unpacking and exploration. For example, if you look at the proportion of children referred to GIDS who were looked-after children, they are over-represented in trans-identifying adolescence by a factor of eight.

I am not aware of any research that shows that experience of care would be over-represented in people who are lesbian, gay and bisexual. I may be wrong, but I am not aware of any research that shows that.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Isn’t the answer support and open conversation, rather than treating those conversations as conversion practices?

evidence.quote: Is the solution to that challenge of the experience of young trans people not the need for support and open conversation, rather than what might be defined as conversion practice?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I agree they need support and conversation. My concern is that the definition might include a mother helping a 13-year-old who identifies as a boy to feel comfortable in her body. I think that could encourage social transition, which may in turn make a medical route more likely.

evidence.quote: I absolutely agree that they should have support and ongoing conversation, but I think the risk is that the definition of “conversion practices” in the Bill is so widely drawn that it encapsulates ordinary parenting and ordinary conversation

if you are making a conversion practice out of, for example, a conversation that a mother might have with a 13-year-old girl who identifies as a boy, and you make it illegal for that mother to help that child feel comfortable in her body, you are effectively embedding a social transition pathway in law, which potentially leads to a more concrete identity

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: I still don’t see how that shows a conversion practice is taking place. And I disagree with treating sexual orientation as stable and measurable while treating trans identity as something different: people’s understanding of their sexual orientation develops too.

evidence.quote: Why is that directly relevant to whether a conversion practice is taking place? I understand what you are saying about the journey of trans communities and what they may experience in life, but how does that directly relate to the case in point of this legislation?
We will agree to disagree. I think people’s understanding of sexual orientation develops. Fundamentally, sexual orientation and trans identity are both identities

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I see sexual orientation as something that can be assessed through attraction, behaviour and identity. Gender identity, as I understand it, relies on a person’s account of their own sense of who they are; I don’t think there’s the same objective measure.

evidence.quote: Sexual orientation is measurable by behaviour, attraction and identity, whereas transgender identity is only about a sense of who you are, for which you cannot have an objective measure. It relies entirely on self-report.
sexual orientation is defined across three different axes: attraction, behaviour and identity.

chapters.title: What family courts can already do
chapters.takeaway: Existing law can protect children from serious harm, but the witnesses identified possible value in naming conversion practices and allowing preventive orders.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: The Bill doesn’t define “abusive”. Would families have to wait for court cases to establish what it means?

evidence.quote: In previous evidence, it has been suggested that individuals might need to go through the process of going to court in order to define what is meant by “abusive”.
Is this something that happens elsewhere in family law, or indeed in criminal law, involving children?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Family courts already know how to apply “significant harm”, because legislation and past decisions explain it. “Abusive” would need its own body of decisions. If the Bill instead said conduct that causes or is likely to cause significant harm, family lawyers would know what test to use.

evidence.quote: We have very clearly defined terms in the Children Act that we use, such as “significant harm”. There is a body of case law that establishes what “significant harm” means.
When you are looking at the word “abusive”, with the Act as defined, you would have to have a body of case law that established what that meant.

If the language was more in line with the language that we use in the family courts—not “abusive”, but “conduct that causes or is likely to cause significant harm”—we would very much be clear about what was meant.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: I agree. People working in family law and child protection use familiar tests. Parts of these definitions are broad and open to interpretation, which makes them harder to apply.

evidence.quote: the terminology and the definition are very unfamiliar to family practitioners because we are used to working within certain terms and thresholds that local authorities use, for example, to initiate child protection processes
the definitions here are quite wide in some aspects and subject to interpretation, which is not what we are used to.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: Suppose parents repeatedly subject their 14-year-old gay son to religious deliverance sessions, deprive him of sleep and isolate him from friends. Could family law protect him now?

evidence.quote: Let us say parents subject their 14-year-old gay son to repeated deliverance sessions, sleep deprivation and isolation from friends. Would that be a criminal act? At the moment, would family law deal with that?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Yes. In my view, that would meet the significant-harm test, allowing a court to make a care order or put the family under supervision. But local authorities can’t currently apply for the particular preventive orders proposed in this Bill.

evidence.quote: That would constitute, in my view, significant harm attributable to the care provided by the parents
That would therefore trigger the court to have jurisdiction to make care orders, which could remove that child, or supervision orders
It would not give the local authority the ability to apply for protective orders, which are contained within the schedule to the Act

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: What if parents plan to send their 15-year-old abroad for a conversion programme? Is there a gap there?

evidence.quote: My second scenario is that parents plan to send their 15-year-old child abroad for a conversion programme. Would the existing law be able to deal with that, or is there a gap in the law?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: A local authority could seek to remove the child or supervise the family if the significant-harm test were met. A High Court injunction might theoretically stop the trip, but I haven’t found an example. I think there’s a gap for the kind of preventive order this Bill proposes.

evidence.quote: A local authority has the ability to intervene and remove the child into foster care, if the test for significant harm or the likelihood of significant harm is met, or to support them through supervision orders.
there is a gap around the preventative order that we see in the schedule to the Act.
Injunctions could theoretically be made, but Parliament has not told the courts what to do, and since we are engaged in this process, we can say there is a gap there.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Could using family-law tests in this Bill confuse the different jobs of family and criminal courts?

evidence.quote: Do you not think there is a danger of using those to perhaps identify a gap and to confuse family law and criminal law approaches?
do we have a danger in confusing criminal law and family law approaches? What would your recommendation to us be?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: If Parliament wants family courts to make these orders, it should say plainly what test those courts must apply. For children, I suggest conversion practices that cause or are likely to cause significant harm. I’m not offering a view on the Bill’s criminal-law test.

evidence.quote: I will not talk about the criminal law aspects of the Bill, because they are outside my expertise.

if you want the family court to be engaged with making orders that protect children from a type of harm that you have identified on a policy basis, I really do not understand why you do not say, in the schedule or elsewhere in the Bill, that the family court has the power to make these orders. The test might be conversion practices that cause or are likely to cause significant harm.
If you want the family courts to make orders, I suggest you have something in the Bill that says, “Within the family court, this is the test,”

turns.speaker: Olivia Bailey
turns.text: Even if other laws can address some of these harms, would naming conversion practices help professionals recognise them and help courts prevent them?

evidence.quote: because they are quite complex in their nature and can often involve multiple harms, there is a challenge with professionals and maybe social workers identifying those harms and recognising the problem.
Do you agree that, without that definition, it could be hard for prosecutions to be made and for professionals to recognise and spot potential abuse?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: Yes. Naming a practice makes clear what the law is addressing, rather than fitting it into several existing offences. If Parliament decides to outlaw it, a specific law could also let courts stop it before it happens, as happens with forced marriage and female genital mutilation.

evidence.quote: There is something about naming; if you make the policy decision that these types of practices need to be outlawed, and if you name it, instead of trying to fit it into a number of different offences, then it is clear.

With forced marriage and female genital mutilation, the inclusion of a separate Act that outlawed something that was already outlawed allowed the court to make orders that are preventative in nature, rather than waiting for the offence to have been committed and then prosecuting.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Silvertown
turns.text: Have you seen authorities act against parents over conversion practices? I found, as an MP, that getting authorities to recognise what was happening could be difficult.

evidence.quote: do you, Sarah or Shabana, know of any action that has been taken against a parent for participation in or commission of a conversion practice? From my experience as a local MP some years ago, it was very difficult to get the authorities to recognise what was happening and take any action at all.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: I found few reported cases directly on this. I did find one where a court placed a child with his father after finding that his mother was imposing a belief that he was trans without evidence. Not all family cases are reported, so I can’t say how often related issues arise.

evidence.quote: I have spent quite a lot of time looking at whether there are reported cases on this specific point, and it is difficult to find any.
the mother was imposing her belief that her son was trans, when there was no evidence that her son was trans. The court in that circumstance made a care order and placed the child with the father.
not every case is reported.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: In my practice, I haven’t come across a case where a local authority couldn’t use existing family-court powers to protect a child.

evidence.quote: In my years of practice, I have never come across a case in which the local authority has found itself unable to exercise the current jurisdiction or to encourage the court to exercise the current jurisdiction that it has to protect a child.

chapters.title: Could families become afraid to talk?
chapters.takeaway: Some witnesses feared complaints and uncertainty would silence useful conversations; Johnson argued that the Bill’s tests exclude ordinary parenting.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: What could happen to a parent or teacher who’s investigated after a complaint, even if they’re never convicted?

evidence.quote: Can you talk us through the potential consequences of a parent or teacher, etc, being investigated over a safeguarding concern, even if they are not ultimately convicted?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I worry that complaints, including during disputes between separated parents, could make a parent hold back from talking about gender identity. An order could also affect contact with a child. That might harm the warm but firm parenting I believe children need.

evidence.quote: in the case of family breakdown, it could be parents trying to place protection orders against other parents.
One is obviously the high-level risk that a parent loses contact with their child, but I think that there is a chilling effect within the family as well
If you have a teenager who identifies as transgender, it removes a whole swathe of conversation that is possible within the home
authoritative parenting, which is a version of parenting that combines high warmth with high boundaries and limits

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Separated parents may worry that ordinary family discussions will be seen as improperly controlling their child’s views. That concern could inhibit those discussions.

evidence.quote: I agree with what Matilda said about this inhibiting of parental discussions, particularly when parents have separated, which are the cases that we deal with. The natural discussions that would take place within families could potentially be prohibited or controlled in some way because parents are worried about falling within the definition of exerting unreasonable controls over the views their children may be expressing.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The Bill could simply say it doesn’t prohibit open-ended discussion, professional assessment or advice that doesn’t aim at a particular identity. Even if lawyers think those conversations wouldn’t meet all the Bill’s tests, a worried social worker might still feel unable to do their job.

evidence.quote: why does the Bill not say that? In the definition of conversion practices, why do you not just say, “This is not intended to prohibit open-ended exploration, assessment and advice”.
we are talking about social workers who are worried about breaking the law having a conversation with a child in care, who has been sexually abused, about their identity.
If the effect on the individual is that they feel like they cannot do their job, then make it clearer.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: I disagree that the Bill threatens normal, messy parenting. It targets conduct intended to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity, which must also meet tests of abuse and serious harm or distress affecting daily life. I’ve found no evidence that comparable bans have produced a surge of complaints against parents, though I encourage the committee to check directly with those places.

evidence.quote: This is not normal backwards and forwards between parents and their children.
This Bill specifically seeks to address a compulsion—an extreme reaction—in a minority of parents who feel compelled to change the sexual orientation or gender identity of their child.
Distress, by the way, is “serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities.”

I also encourage the Committee to seek evidence from jurisdictions that already have comprehensive, trans-inclusive conversion practices bans and ask those jurisdictions for evidence on whether they have seen a spike in vexatious claims against parents, religious figures or therapists. I have had a look and I can find zero evidence that that is the case.
Even if it were, you then have the two additional tests of proven abusive as a matter of fact, followed by “serious harm” or “serious alarm and distress” as effects.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: Could a child ultimately be removed from home if a parent were accused under this Bill?

evidence.quote: what is the likelihood of a child—this is for CAFCASS in particular—ultimately being removed from their parents if the parent is accused of an offence under this Bill?

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: An accusation might prompt a child-protection inquiry, but removal wouldn’t be automatic. The local authority would assess the risk and could ask the family court either to oversee care at home or to place the child in foster care while the case proceeds. I can’t predict an outcome without that assessment and the court’s decision.

evidence.quote: Perhaps if they were notified that a parent had been accused of this, that would then start the child protection inquiry

they would apply in the usual way for a protective order for that child, either for them to oversee the child’s placement at home by making an interim care order and allowing the local authority to exercise parental responsibility over that child, or by removing that child into a foster care placement while proceedings were ongoing
I cannot give a definitive answer. It would much depend on the local authority’s risk assessment—and the court’s view

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Does the Bill clearly leave room for legitimate conversations between parents and teenagers?

evidence.quote: are the Bill’s measures drawn sufficiently tightly to avoid capturing legitimate parental conversations?

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: In our view, yes. The Bill doesn’t force a parent to affirm a child’s identity. A parent could, for example, refuse to buy a chest binder out of concern about its health effects. That isn’t, in my view, conduct intended to change the child’s identity, let alone conduct meeting the Bill’s further tests.

evidence.quote: we do not believe there is anything in the Bill that compels a parent to affirm or accept their child’s sexual orientation or gender identity.

If the child says, “I want you to buy me a binder to cope with my gender distress”, it is entirely reasonable for a parent to say, “I am very worried about the health impacts of that. That’s not something that I support. I accept that you are who you tell me you are, but that is not an action that I will willingly support and fund.”
I don’t think anybody reasonably would argue that is conduct intended to change. Even if it were, you then have the two additional tests

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I disagree. Parents might reasonably help a child explore whether trauma or discomfort with gender stereotypes is involved. Ordinary rules about money or behaviour could be described as emotional or financial pressure. I accept the Bill sets a fairly high bar for distress affecting daily life, but I still think it risks drawing in complicated family situations.

evidence.quote: it might be reasonable for a parent to want to help a 15-year-old girl who has been sexually assaulted and wants to identify out of her body because she no longer feels safe in it, for example, to feel comfortable in her body rather than in a transgender identification
You could remove pocket money for staying out late, which is financial pressure.
I know that there is a reasonably high bar there in terms of it having to have an effect on day-to-day functioning
You risk making it incredibly difficult for parents and potentially creating divisions between parents and their children through the provisions in this Bill.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: A short explanation in the Bill of what’s allowed could help people who aren’t lawyers understand it. Would the rest of you support that?

evidence.quote: I am very keen that wording in legislation is easily interpretable by people who are also not lawyers.
Sarah's suggestion of a clarification—perhaps, a one-line clarification—in the Bill would be really helpful
I just wanted to get the rest of the panel’s opinion on whether they would support the kind of clarification that Sarah has suggested.

turns.speaker: Des Johnson
turns.text: Yes. Clarifying that the Bill targets attempts to change someone, not other conversations, would help.

evidence.quote: Yes.
The abusive practice here lies in the intent to change and what flows from that. So, I think that anything that helps to clarify that that is what the Bill is targeting would be a helpful thing.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: Clarification would help, but I don’t think one line is enough. I’d want much tighter wording about children and their developing identities, particularly where gender identity is concerned.

evidence.quote: a clarification would be helpful, but I also think that it does not go far enough, because you would still get massive unintended consequences with the wide drafting of the other parts of the Bill, particularly when you are talking about children and young people shifting identities
It would also require within the legislation a very tight definition that makes it clear what applies to adults, and to consider children’s safeguarding as well

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Similar laws exist abroad. What evidence is there that they’ve stopped parents having supportive conversations?

evidence.quote: To what extent has there been a chilling effect? To what extent has good parenting stopped in those countries as a result of this legislation, in your experiences?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: In my research, five interviews were with clinicians in places that already have bans. They told me the laws affected their work and parents’ ability to talk openly. Parenting wasn’t the main focus of that research, though; it came up alongside the clinicians’ experiences.

evidence.quote: five of the interviews were with clinicians working in jurisdictions that already have conversion practice bans. They were very clear about the chilling effects both in terms of their own work and on parents.
My particular piece of research focused on clinicians, and parenting was brought up more as a kind of by the by rather than as the key focus of the report, but it was definitely mentioned.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: We haven’t received that evidence. Please send the committee the cases you’re referring to.

evidence.quote: That is not evidence we have received, so perhaps you could send us the evidence of those parents who are not able to parent in those jurisdictions.
It would be helpful if you could share them.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Despite your concerns about this Bill, do you agree abusive conversion practices can happen?

evidence.quote: from your research, you agree that there have been and continue to be abusive conversion practices?

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I’m sure they happen and think they’re wrong, though I haven’t personally seen evidence of them. I’m uncertain how common they are because some research hasn’t defined the practice clearly. I also think much of what people would call abuse is already illegal.

evidence.quote: I have not seen evidence of abusive conversion practices, but I am sure they happen. My understanding is that what most of us understand to be abusive conversion practices are already prohibited under existing law.
Some of it that looks at the prevalence of conversion practices did not actually define conversion practices
At that point, we do not know how prevalent actual conversion practices are. Again, I am sure they happen. They are entirely wrong and they should not happen

chapters.title: Orders to prevent harm
chapters.takeaway: The family-law witnesses saw potential value in preventive orders, while urging safeguards against misuse and unnecessarily broad restrictions.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Could a parent use an application for a conversion-practice protection order against the other parent during a dispute about their child?

evidence.quote: Are you worried about parents using the child as a weapon, effectively, against the other parent?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: I’d change the application rules so people outside the listed groups must first get the court’s permission. That would let a judge examine why they’re applying, rather than treating permission as a formality.

evidence.quote: It would be better framed along the lines of the section 91(14) of the Children Act, which says that no party may bring an application “without leave of the court.” That shifts the emphasis and deals with vexatious claims.
You have to engage with what the motivation behind this is.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Yes, there’s a real risk of bringing children into another part of a dispute between their parents.

evidence.quote: It is a real concern that children may be brought into yet another aspect of a parental dispute. That is one of the unintended consequences of the current drafting.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: I’d look to orders used to prevent forced marriage and female genital mutilation. In my experience, those can sometimes keep a child safely with their family when the alternative would be removal into care. Because these new orders could be complicated, I’d also have full-time judges handle them.

evidence.quote: I think we can learn from FGM orders and forced marriage orders.
these sorts of orders are best dealt with by full-time judges. The Bill does not specify.
when the extra powers of these preventive orders were introduced, you could often keep children within the family with these orders in place, which mitigated significant harm.
If you have a family who are law-abiding and would comply with orders, that might help to keep families together.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Such orders may be temporary while the court works out the risk. A long restriction on travel can also bring a family back to court later when they need to travel for an ordinary reason.

evidence.quote: forced marriage protection orders and FGM orders tend to be interim and a holding position until you have established what the risk is.
The travel abroad components often cause an issue if they are made for a lengthy period, because obviously families want to travel from time to time.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The Bill’s appeal rule also needs explaining. It appears to let someone who wasn’t part of the original case appeal an order, but doesn’t say who that person could be or why they’d be entitled to appeal.

evidence.quote: You have a provision that says that someone else who is not a party to the proceedings can bring an appeal, but there is no clarity about who. We can talk about vexatious appeals. Who is entitled to appeal an order if they are not a party? You had better tell us.

turns.speaker: Matilda Gosling
turns.text: I’m also worried that an order concerning gender identity might have no clear limit on what a court could require. I fear a parent could be pressed to support social transition or pay for a binder against their judgment.

evidence.quote: there is no obvious limit that can be placed on the court as to what they can instruct. That potentially means that a parent might be compelled into social transition, paying for breast binders and other things that they may not feel are compatible with their duties, rights and responsibilities as a parent.

chapters.title: Children and a stretched court system
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses asked Parliament to clarify whether children could face the Bill’s criminal offence and to plan for the work it might create.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What might this Bill mean for family courts and services for young people?

evidence.quote: Can you give us some idea of the impact that this Bill, when it comes into effect, will have on the family law system in general—particularly the family court system—and on the services provided to young people?

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The courts are already overburdened: some family cases take a year or more to reach a final hearing. More orders mean more preparation for lawyers and court time. If Parliament creates that work, it needs to pay for it.

evidence.quote: Courts are overburdened. Private law proceedings now have waits of a year or more to get the case to final hearing.
If these orders are made within existing family law proceedings, for example, you as a barrister or solicitor will have extra work and preparation and it would not be remunerated.
If you are going to make more work for the family courts, resource it and make sure that it is properly dealt with.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: Local authorities and family courts are already under pressure and going through changes. The Bill might lead to more child-protection referrals or court cases, but I can’t say how many.

evidence.quote: The family law jurisdiction is under pressure from a number of sides. There is also a lot of reform happening within family law at the moment.
there could potentially be an increase in safeguarding referrals.
We cannot say exactly how much that would increase
we may see an increase in these types of cases coming before the court.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Bill applies to children as well as adults. Could a child accused of trying to change someone else’s identity be drawn into the criminal offence?

evidence.quote: it applies equally to children as to adults. It is possible that a child could be brought in as somebody who has engaged in abusive conversive practices.

turns.speaker: Sarah Branson
turns.text: The age of criminal responsibility is 10. Parliament needs to decide whether it intends 10- or 11-year-olds to be covered. If not, the Bill should say so clearly.

evidence.quote: It is right that the criminal age of responsibility is 10. It is up to you to make a policy decision about whether you expect 10 and 11-year-olds to be criminalised as a result of trying to change. If you do not, then you need to make it clearer.

turns.speaker: Shabana Jaffar
turns.text: I agree. The draft doesn’t say what would happen to a child in that situation, and that concerns me.

evidence.quote: I agree. The Bill as drafted is currently silent on the potential consequences for a child in that scenario and that is a concern.
